name: Name
title: by Orrin Grey and Sherwin Matthews

name: Name
body:
The line of thralls threading their way through the tunnel paused as the party reached the cave mouth, various armaments clicking and buzzing quietly in the dark. At their head, the skarlock leading them cast its glowing eyes about in the moonlight, surveying the valley stretching out before them.
A small village was nestled in the craw of the land below, a dozen domed huts clustered tight against a dark stand of trees. A large communal fire burned in the pit between the buildings, illuminating several figures at rest, eating their evening meal, and talking amongst themselves. Some of the smaller trollkin dozed, cradled in the arms of their parents.
The skarlock simply observed for a time, assessing the next course of action. The thralls numbered just over thirty in total, easily the match of the trollkin. It did not perceive any defenses at the settlement perimeter, nor the presence of armed warriors. The trollkin were an easy target, relaxed and unaware of the danger at hand.
Even so, the skarlock considered moving on.

name: Name
body:
The creature’s master had set it two missions. The first was acquisition of resources. The construction site required a constant influx of raw materials; necrotite, stone, machinery, and corpses to create new thralls. The second mission was scouting. Ancient cephalyx tunnels wove their way through the Alchiere subcontinent, passages dug so long ago that no living creature could recall where they emerged or how they connected. Mapping these trails was vital for establishing transportation of construction materials.
This village offered limited salvage opportunity. Trollkin tended to avoid old battle sites where necrotite had gathered when making their settlements, and the rustic folk rarely possessed much by way of machinery. With so small a population, the village would provide few bodies. Yet, the skarlock reasoned, with surprise on the Cryxian side it would also offer little resistance, and the small number of materials that were gathered would be unlikely to impair the raiding party’s speed. It had been days since the creature’s force had encountered any living thing except bats and insects. Turning back would entail countless hours of marching. At least if they raided the trollkin village, they would return with something more to show for their efforts than another report of a tunnel that went nowhere.

name: Name
body:
The decision was made. With a simple gesture, the skarlock motioned for the thralls under its command to begin their descent down the rocky slope, toward the settlement and unsuspecting trollkin. The mechanithralls were the swiftest, lighter on their feet than the lumbering brutes, that stomped through the undergrowth with a more measured gait.
The skarlock’s rictus grin widened as it joined the others, quickly reaching the front of the pack. At last it saw a sentry, a dozing trollkin lounging on a large rock, a spear leaned against his shoulder. The skarlock cast out one bony claw and chattered a command, and the guard was immolated by a burst of black flame.
The thralls were not stealthy, but nonetheless, their presence went undetected under cover of darkness until the raiding party swarmed through the village. Armed as they were with an array of claws, blades, and buzzsaws, the mechanithralls made short work of the villagers they encountered, and began to carve their way through the wattle and daub walls of the huts in search of the cowering figures within.

name: Name
body:
Screams echoed through the clearing, quickly silenced until all that remained was the clanking sound of the thralls as they prowled about in search of survivors. The skarlock paused to survey its troops, and observed that only a single mechanithrall had been felled, decapitated by a stout trollkin woman wielding a large machete. Her corpse lay a few feet away from the kill, flank split open by a buzzsaw’s blade and a deep pool of her blood soaking into the soil beneath. It was an acceptable exchange. Mechanithralls were expendable by design, and the trollkin’s flesh would be harvested.
With the slaughter over, the remaining thralls began to pick their way through the village, gathering resources for their masters.
***

name: Name
body:
"Another dead village up ahead, Sarge." Dutch spat his disgust on the ground. "The bastard rotters took everything, just like the one we found before. Not a trace of the civies that lived there, beyond a few bloody stains."
Sergeant Hulder Craghorn took a deep breath, closing his eyes and shaking his head. It was a familiar gesture to the troops under his command. They all shared his frustration. Sensing his master’s growing ire through their bond, Klangor gnashed his teeth and stared about for something to smash.
Six weeks had passed since the Baying Wolf  had been sighted and boarded, and the news of Admiral Boomhowler’s death had rocked the Southern Kriels. Five weeks since the Kithguard had begun operations under direct orders from the great chieftain Madrak Ironhide. In that time, they had found little trace of the Cryxian threat—only empty settlements.
The question of how the Cryxians had reached the interior of the Southern Kriels without any naval invasion or beach landings was only overshadowed by the mystery of why they were in Alchiere at all. Yet, the trollkin knew without any doubt the Cryxians were in their midst. The disappearances were too clinical and too precise to be the work of beasts. And wherever an empty village was found, the air was rank with the foul stench of thrall—rotting flesh and machinery twisted in hellish concert.

name: Name
body:
But, with no targets to strike, all the Kithguard could do was to patrol the interior, checking in with each settlement they found, and scouting for any trace of the enemy.
Craghorn looked to the sky, where the steadily falling sun had almost disappeared from sight behind the trees. It had been a long day of marching. The territory in this region was untamed swampland, forcing them at times to wade through murky water that reached their waist, and on drier land tackle increasingly dense foliage. He didn’t need to look at his soldiers to know they were all tired. He felt it too. The prospect of digging through yet another ghost town didn’t fill him with much enthusiasm at the best of times, let alone now.
He sighed. Their fatigue was unimportant. They had their orders, and couldn’t just leave the settlement be. "Take me to the village. We’ll secure the perimeter and camp there for the night."
The distance wasn’t far, but by the time they arrived, still kicking swamp water from their boots, the surrounding jungle was painted in hues of amber. The warm color did little to dispel the unease that settled in Craghorn’s stomach. It was the same each time he witnessed one of these abandoned settlements.

name: Name
body:
It seemed there was little left to investigate. As Dutch had already identified, the only traces of the villagers were a smattering of bloodstains, predominantly around the central hearth. Several of the buildings had been broken into, their interiors exposed to the elements and the wind whistling eerily through the gaps.
Due to the nature of the patrols, general Gunnbjorn had taken the decision to break up his forces in smaller scouting parties. As such, Craghorn was in command of a relatively small complement, made up of a handful of hardened irregulars who had fought by his side time and time again. The Scrappers, brutal guerilla fighters whose pickaxes and concussion charges were as capable of bringing down a warjack as making short work of enemy soldiers. Private Rattles, the pyg Tunnel Rat who had saved Craghorn’s life several times over. Corporal Rhud Felleye, the best sniper that Craghorn had ever known, served as their pathfinder. The final member of their party was of course, Klangor, Craghorn’s loyal companion. Craghorn couldn’t imagine going into battle without the hulking dire troll—and he was reasonably sure that even if he tried to leave the dire troll behind, Klangor would have torn a path through the jungle to get to his side once more.

name: Name
body:
Every one of them was used to sleeping rough and eating cold, but Craghorn didn’t see any sense in depriving them or taking any unnecessary hits to the unit’s morale. On missions like this, far from home, it was important to keep spirits up.
Dutch and Annar built a fire in the hearth, then Dyhllan began to cook some game they had left over from the previous day. Before long, the flames where beating back the descending night, and the smell of roasting meat floated through the air.
"My folks came from a village like this," Annar gestured around them with a bone she’d already picked clean of meat. "Up near the Bloodsmeath Marsh, though we had left it behind by the time I came along. My ma was always talking about it, though. Wind rippling through the reeds, that kind of thing. Not sure how you make a swamp sound romantic, but she could do it."
Felleye was chewing on a piece of long grass, still letting his portion of the meal cool. "You get used to it," he replied, his voice a slow, quiet drawl. "Then, you get to where you miss it."

name: Name
body:
In a lot of ways, Felleye was an opposite to Craghorn. Quiet and softspoken, and a devout Dhunian. While he was as effective a killer as Craghorn had ever fought alongside, he didn’t seem to share his commanding officer’s attraction to battle. In some ways, Craghorn thought that was probably for the best.
"Did we ever hear where you hail from?" Dyhllan asked.
"Fenn Marsh," Felleye said, before sensing Klangor’s eyes on his meal and at last taking a measured bite. "Down near Clocker’s Cove, Gulf of Cygnar. That’s where I learned to hunt."
Dutch laughed. "Well, in that case, swamp’s gotta be worth something."
While the others talked, Rattles had taken his rations and dug himself a hole a little distance away from the rest and disappeared, as was his wont. None of them took offence at the eccentric pygmy troll. They were more than used to it.
Klangor had long wolfed his meal down and since captured something else to eat, although exactly what this creature might have once been was too difficult to tell. Craghorn watched as the dire troll cracked open a large shell of some description, and stuffed a handful of broken shards and bloody flesh into his mouth.

name: Name
body:
"Not sure you should be eating that," Craghorn winced at the horrendous crunching noises, and offered a word of caution as Klangor stuffed another quivering chunk of flesh into his gullet. "Whatever it is could be poisonous."
Klangor belched by way of reply, but seemed otherwise unfazed, leaving Craghorn to question whether the dire troll had even understood the words.
They drew straws for watches, Dyhllan walking over to Rattles’ hole and sticking the fistful of sticks into the soil for the pyg to draw one. Craghorn wasn’t sad to draw first watch. A lifetime spent in the service had taught him how to sleep just about anywhere, and at just about any time an opportunity allowed itself. Nonetheless, he expected to have difficulty drifting off that night. Of late, his mind chewed at itself when he wasn’t in combat. Amidst the lonely village and its ghosts, he knew he’d find little peace and need exhaustion on his side.
The conversation faded to a murmur as the fire burned low, and the others bedded down. Rattles remained in his hole, and the Scrappers took themselves off to one of the abandoned huts. Nearby, Klangor pillowed his huge head on one of the bombs he carried and was almost immediately asleep. The dire troll resembled little more than a pile of sharp rocks, except for his loud snoring.

name: Name
body:
Craghorn found a wide stone to perch on at the edge of the village, and looked back the way they’d come. From his elevated position he could see the swamp stretching out for miles under the moonlight, mist rising up from the surface as the air above the water cooled. In contrast to the ominous village behind, it was a soothing sight.
Felleye wordlessly settled beside him. For a time the pair didn’t speak, each lost to their own thoughts.
"There’s a saying where I come from." Felleye’s voice, soft but no less assertive for it, was the first to break the silence. "It had a few variations, but the one I heard most often was, ‘spend too much time indoors, and you neglect the garden.’"
Craghorn had heard it before, while part of the bandit troupe. Stay out of the fight for too long, and you’ll get soft. He turned his attention to the sniper, one eye ridge raised.
Felleye stared ahead of him, eyes boring into the night. "The trollkin have always fought. As Molgur, then kriels, against the reds and the swans. So much of our past is defined by struggle. We came here to find peace. But what if peace has made us weak? We’re children of the Wurm, as well as the Great Mother."

name: Name
body:
Craghorn found he didn’t have an answer for that. Or perhaps, he didn’t want to answer that.
Felleye turned to Craghorn. "We’ll find the rotters. The people of these villages need to be avenged. Boomhowler needs to be avenged." His stare was hard, eyes piercing Craghorn in place. The silence between them stretched out for just a moment longer, then Felleye retired, leaving Craghorn to his thoughts.
***

name: Name
body:
Craghorn abruptly awoke at the sound of a shrill whistle, a piercing call used throughout the Kithguard to sound the alarm. Half a second later, he became aware of shouting and gunfire echoing through the village. He made it to his feet like Gunnbjorn himself had given the order, seizing both Daisy and Vulcan as he charged out of the hut he’d taken shelter in.
At first, he couldn’t tell who the enemy were or their numbers, only a series of large figures loping through the village, their shoulders hunched low to the ground. Craghorn hit Vulcan’s ignition switch and the maul burst into flames, illuminating several gatormen, their reptilian hides unmistakable in the light. The sudden brightness caused the nearby attackers to recoil, their eyes squinting and slow to adjust.
Craghorn had fought gatorfolk before, and knew they could be as tough and cantankerous as a full blood troll, and twice as cunning. Like most of their kind, they wore little in the way of accoutrements, trusting to their thick hides for protection. Each of them bore a rusted polearm, but even without their weapons, they were a dangerous foe. Their lashing tails and sharp teeth were plenty deadly.

name: Name
body:
Klangor was still stirring as Craghorn reached into his mind. At Craghorn’s mental urging, the dire troll blinked away the cobwebs and fished into his pack, producing one of the bombs it always carted around. Still sluggish, it hurled the explosive shell in the direction of the gators, and it detonated in their midst, hurling scaly hides and chunks of muddy earth against the walls.
Before the dust could settle, Craghorn opened fire at the remaining gatormen, lighting up the night in staccato bursts. Shooting into this foe was like firing at a living wall. Far from being forced back, the gatormen roared defiantly and charged toward him. A rusty blade gashed his side, and he jerked his shoulder back just in time to avoid a pair of snapping jaws. He let Daisy sag in the strap and switched to Vulcan, driving the top of the maul under the gullet of the gator who had just tried to bite his arm off. A gout of flame cooked the soft part of the gator’s throat, and boiled its eyes in their sockets.

name: Name
body:
As Craghorn shoved the gatorman’s thrashing body away, he was too late to block a thrust by one of its companions, the heavy blade catching him in the upper arm. Daisy swung wildly and unbalanced Craghorn, but before his assailant could capitalize, one of Felleye’s bullets split the gatorman’s skull.
The others were on their feet now. The Scrappers roared a challenge as they rushed to get to grips with the swamp beasts, hurling grenades over their heads to land amongst the press of scaly flesh. Klangor lumbered behind their assault. Like any dire troll, Klangor would have been deadly with his fists and teeth alone, but he was armed with more than just that. The massive blade in his hand was as at home slicing through scales as it was chopping through dense jungle foliage.
It was hard to estimate exactly how many foes there were. They lashed and thrust and snapped with surprising speed and unsurprising ferocity, but gave way before the exuberance of the dire troll. Tough as they were, the gatormen were no match for Klangor, even more outmatched by the presence of Craghorn and his soldiers also. Just as quickly as it had begun, the tide of the battle turned.

name: Name
body:
As the gatormen began to fall back, a voice shouted above the din in barely recognizable Cygnaran. "Parley!" The voice was thick and guttural, reminding Craghorn of the Southern Kriels’ bullcroak allies, though this sounded rougher, as though the speaker was talking through a mouthful of rocks or broken teeth.
For a heartbeat, Craghorn considered allowing Klangor continue his slaughter. The gatormen were on the retreat, and pausing might give them a chance to regroup. Nonetheless, against his better judgement he called a halt to his troops, and with some difficulty, managed to subdue and rein in Klangor.
"Parley." he replied.
The leader of the gatormen stepped forward from among the press of reptilian bodies. Where most gatormen could have been taken for regular beasts if they put down their weapons and lay on their bellies, there was no mistaking this one. It wore a patchwork cloak in an array of motley colors, and a circlet decorated with several colorful feathers, each taken from one variety of swamp bird or another.

name: Name
body:
"Seen your kind before, friend." The gatorman had a strange accent, unlike anything Craghorn had encountered before. "They were pirates. That is what pirates say? Parley?"
"It is," Craghorn agreed, "but we aren’t pirates." Craghorn had seen this gator’s kind before, too. It had to be a bokor—the spiritual leaders of the gatorfolk who, unlike their fellows, had a tendency toward ostentation in their sartorial choices. "Why would you parley? You attacked us."
The gatorman made a theatrical effort of dipping its head. "Followed the intruders to our swamp. Thought we would find an easy meal. We were…" it searched for a word, "…mistaken."
"So you’d like us to let bygones be bygones?" Craghorn was far from convinced. While the creature might be speaking the truth, the gatormen could just as easily have intended to attack the village.
The bokor’s eyes narrowed. "Troll meat is tough meat, friend. We have come out of this worse than you."
Craghorn felt his lip curl upward in a grim smile. "So you have. I’ll make you a deal. We can call this a misunderstanding and let you walk away. But first, I have questions."

name: Name
body:
The bokor considered for a moment and then shrugged. "You have a deal." It turned to the nearest gatorman and barked an order, half hiss and the rest raspy cough. The bokor’s minion nodded and gave a further order to the remaining gatormen, who lowered their weapons and began to filter out of the village. "What do you want to know, friend?"
"Did you take the people from this village?"
The gatorman hissed. "No. The dead ones took them." It spat the name. It seemed there was no love lost between the gatormen and the Cryxian invaders. The animosity made sense to Craghorn. The magic practiced by the gatormen was a form of necromancy, but centered on the release of life energies at point of death, utterly alien to the cold Cryxian view of corpses as resources.
Alternatively, Craghorn considered, the Cryxian invaders might simply have attacked the village before the gatormen could, and ruined their plans. He decided to ignore that thought for the time being. He believed the gatormen hadn’t attacked the village. Even with several of the huts broken into, it was too clean to be their work. This was the first halfway decent lead the Kithguard had, and there was no sense in squandering it creating a new foes.

name: Name
body:
"Do you know where the Cryxians took them?"
"Not into the water. Most likely to the mountains, friend."
Knowing the Cryxians were avoiding the swamps narrowed down the possible routes they might have taken. The land away from the water was nigh on inhospitable, and prohibitive to a raiding party unless they hacked through and left an obvious trail behind.
"Have you seen the Cryxians elsewhere?"
"In the mountains. We see green lights moving around at night." The bokor bared its teeth in a feral grin, and Craghorn was immediately reminded that this creature was a cold-blooded predator, first and foremost. "They fear our swamps."
One of the trollkin standing behind Craghorn snorted. He chose to ignore it. "Last one. What guarantee do we have that you won’t attack our villages again?"
The bokor broke out into a rough hacking sound, its jaw clacking up and down. Craghorn was bemused by the reaction, until he realized that the creature was laughing.
"You don’t, friend." The gatorman finally composed itself. "But enemy of enemy can be friend… for now."

name: Name
body:
Craghorn didn’t like that much. He also knew he didn’t have much choice. "Fine. But know if you come for our villages, we will be waiting." Riled by Craghorn’s irritation, Klangor uttered a low growl. Something like fear flickered over the bokor’s expression, and Craghorn had the satisfaction of watching the gatorman beat a hasty retreat.
***

name: Name
body:
The mist from the night before continued into the morning, draped over the jungle like a heavy shroud. When he first came to Alchiere, Craghorn had found it and the sense of quietude it brought strangely beautiful, a sentiment that had remained with him until now. Here, any hint of romance was replaced with eeriness and isolation. Craghorn felt exposed as he stalked through the mist, despite being able to see the silhouette of the Scrappers foraging ahead, and being able to feel Klangor’s reassuring presence.
He’d had little by way of sleep after the exchange with the bokor. A gatorman blade had torn a hole through his bicep during the assault and the injury hurt like hell beneath the bandage, coloring him in a foul mood. At least he’d borne the worst of the exchange. Dyhllan had a shallow slice across his forearm, and Rattles sported a gash across his temple, but no bones were broken, no major organs damaged, and all of their wounds would heal with a little time.
His injury wasn’t the only thing that remained with him from the night before. Craghorn could still see the severity in Rhud Felleye’s eyes, and had no doubt the sniper had spoken with absolute sincerity. In Craghorn’s experience, the sniper typically kept his cards close to his chest and wore indifference like a badge of honor at all times. That he had felt so compelled to openly voice his mind spoke of the conviction they all felt.

name: Name
body:
Craghorn’s thoughts were interrupted as the sniper appeared from the bush ahead and jogged over. His lips wore a wry smile, and Craghorn didn’t need to hear Felleye’s report to know they at last had their lead.
"Form up, on me." While the members of his unit hastened to his position, Craghorn turned to the sniper.
Felleye didn’t leave him waiting. "The gators had the truth of it. Found a series of tracks heading up the hillside, that lead into a cave mouth. They covered them well. I might not have looked twice, were it not for the remains of a sentry that got scorched."
"They left a corpse behind?" This struck Craghorn as unusual, given their efforts to otherwise hide their tracks.
"Nothing left to leave," came the reply. "Just ash, burned grass, and charred stone. Only things left were the rune tags."
"Hmm. One of ours?"
Felleye shook his head. "Militia. Most of the villages out this far have one or two stationed to watch out for trouble."
Craghorn knew the type. Most likely an older veteran or an aspiring adolescent. Neither had any hope of standing up to a Cryxian patrol on their own.

name: Name
body:
The others had gathered now. Craghorn kept his orders clipped and to the point. "We move. Five yard spread, no sound. Eyes on Felleye." There was little need for further instruction as they trailed the sniper back into the bush and began to ascend the hillside.
The going was steady, although wasn’t steep enough to have them breathing too heavily by the time they cleared the mist. Below the fog spread like a vast ocean as far as the eye could see, only sporadically broken by the canopy, the tallest trees visible as indistinct shapes in the gloom. In contrast the sky above was almost blinding in its brightness. If the cleaner air had done wonders to chase away Craghorn’s mood, the sun burned the sentiment back into his skin.
"Ah din like it." Trailing behind, Rattles broke orders and gave voice to Craghorn’s discomfort. "Too much sky. Anythin’ could see you up here." The pyg had a point, but Craghorn shushed him with a glare all the same.
Up ahead, Felleye paused, one palm held up to signal a halt. He disappeared from sight for a few moments, before reappearing once more and beckoning to follow.

name: Name
body:
Craghorn felt the ground beginning to level out as he climbed to where the sniper had signaled, and realized they had reached an even platform, previously hidden by a patch of dense leaves and long grass. There was still a ways to go to the summit, but it seemed they’d arrived at their destination. A cave mouth awaited in the side of the hill, deep enough for the interior to be lost in darkness.
It was difficult to tell if the opening was naturally formed or had been dug out. Certainly if it was the latter, it had been done some time previous. Vegetation crawled across the surrounding rock, and the surface of the dirt and stone felt dry and dusty. Craghorn peered inside. He could see little beyond vague outlines of stalactites, but felt cool air rushing up to meet him as it flowed through a tunnel.
He turned and addressed Felleye. "You think they came this way?"
Felleye nodded and pointed to an area of dirt by the cave mouth, where the moss had been trampled. "I’ve been following their tracks all the way up. They were less concerned with covering their trail up here."

name: Name
body:
Rattles was sniffing around the entrance. Alone amongst them, he wore a gleeful smile, excited to get underground once more. He pulled one of the candles from his pack, lit it with flint and steel, and plonked it on his helmet. "Time fer me to lead."
Craghorn could just as easily have fired up Vulcan, but suspected discretion was the better approach by far. The pyg’s light would be far better at not giving away their position to any hostiles coming back this way—and with Klangor with them, they’d need every advantage they could get. The concept of creeping around was lost upon the dire troll.
"Take lead, Rattles. The rest of you, keep formation. Felleye, you’re rearguard. I don’t want any surprises."
If Craghorn had worried about needing to dig out the passage so that Klangor could fit, it quickly became obvious he needn’t have worried. The cave quickly gave way to a wide tunnel with a high ceiling, thankfully large enough that Klangor could pass comfortably through, even where it narrowed. Nonetheless, Craghorn let the Scrappers follow directly behind Rattles, so he could concentrate on calming the dire troll’s natural aversion to the enclosed space.

name: Name
body:
The tunnel turned downwards almost immediately, steadily becoming steeper and causing several of their party to lose their footing and scrabble for purchase, until the slope began to soften once more and banked to the east.
"Rattles thinks we’re below the jungle floor now, Sarge." Annar whispered back a message from the front.
They continued for what felt like hours, the only sound their boots scuffing over the densely packed earth, and the occasional chitter from bats overhead. The passage was seldom straight for long, and weaved like a snake. Craghorn wondered whether part of the tunnel had once been formed by an underground river flow, although the notion that the tunnel might be entirely natural had long been disabused. Looking at where roots had broken through the dirt in the walls and ceilings, it was most likely the diggers had expanded the space whilst also avoiding where the deepest roots blocked the way.
"Stop." Once more, Annar’s voice reached Craghorn, although this time her tone held an edge of urgency that had been absent beforehand.

name: Name
body:
Craghorn bade Klangor remain where he was, and then hastened to the front of the line, where Dyhllan, Dutch, and Rattles waited, crouched behind a rock formation with their heads down. He immediately saw why. Unnatural purple light played over the walls from around the next corner, shadows dancing across the uneven rock as the source moved around.
"Cephalyx." Dyhllan replied to his unspoken question in a low voice. "My mother used to tell me stories about them. Stories that her mother had told her, and her mother had told her. Never dreamed I’d see them here."
"I’ve fought them before. Years ago. They get into your head. It isn’t natural." Dutch added.
"Could this be what the gators saw?" Dyhllan whispered. "They didn’t say they’d been up close and personal to identify them."
"Maybe. I’ve seen the cephalyx work with the rotters before, back in the Thornwood. Could be the same here." Craghorn looked at Rattles. "How many?"
The pyg held up six fingers, followed by a single finger, which he tapped on his head.

name: Name
body:
Six slaves, and one mind slaver. Easy pickings. Craghorn used hand signals to alert Felleye, and exerted more than a little effort in forcing Klangor to continue holding his position. It wasn’t easy. The dire troll had sensed the unease of his companions and was keen to follow, but Craghorn was concerned Klangor might bring down the ceiling if he was careless or got too excited.
Keeping their heads down, the party crept along the tunnel until they reached where the corner curved out of sight. Craghorn slowly leant out and risked a glance.
The group of drudges seemed to be occupied with digging out a cave-in. They were covered in sweat and their unnatural muscles bulged as their master, floating to one side, mentally drove them to smash rocks and hurl the shattered pieces aside. Like most drudge slaves Craghorn had seen, the figures seemed to be human. The eye sockets in their helmets blazed with purple light, presumably a result of their master’s domination.
Their distraction was more than enough for Craghorn to motion to the other trollkin, who quietly filed out behind him and readied themselves for Craghorn’s order to attack.

name: Name
body:
Craghorn let Daisy give the order, levelling her at the drudges and opening fire. Rapid muzzle flashes strobed the cave walls as the firearm’s already loud bark became a deafening cacophony. The hail of bullets immediately dropped two of the drudges, reducing the closest to torn up meat, and tearing the legs out from underneath the figure immediately behind. Another span on the spot in a gruesome pirouette before falling bloody in the dirt, one arm missing, but shambled back to its feet, apparently unphased by the hideous wound. Felleye’s rifle elicited a familiar punching sound in response, and a moment later the wounded drudge’s head exploded like ripe fruit.
Driven onwards by their cruel master, the cephalyx’s remaining puppets were upon them. Possessed by an unnatural burst of speed, the first reached Rattles, who rewarded his assailant’s persistence by sinking his pickaxe into their body up to the bone. The Scrappers rushed to the pyg’s aid as the remaining pair of drudges closed on their diminutive ally.

name: Name
body:
Back down the tunnel, Klangor had grown too excited from the noise and commotion to wait any longer, and before Craghorn could stop him, the dire troll bounced into the melee. It shouldered past the Scrappers and clenched a meaty fist around the abdomen of each drudge, and heedless of their struggling, smashed them together over and over, until both were a bloody pulp of ruined flesh and bone.
Craghorn felt a scratching sensation at the edge of his consciousness. Klangor howled and doubled over, releasing the remains of the drudges and clasping his hands to his head. Further down the tunnel the cephalyx floated ominously. The purple light surrounding it grew to blinding in its intensity as the vile creature attempted to wrest control of the dire troll. Craghorn had no idea if such a thing were even possible, but as he tried to calm Klangor, felt the bond between them slipping away.
Ready to open fire at the mind slaver, he stepped forward, just in time to see Dutch rip the pin out of a concussive charge and hurl it down the tunnel toward the cephalyx.

name: Name
body:
The world shook violently, knocking friend and foe from their feet and bringing chunks of earth raining to the floor from above. A high pitched whine took root in Craghorn’s ears, blocking out all other sound and disorientating him for a moment as he frantically looked back and forth to see if the tunnel held. At a quick assessment, it seemed they had been lucky—the only damage was to their senses, judging from how they all shook their heads to clear themselves of the ringing sound.
Incredibly, the cephalyx was the first to rise, albeit unsteadily. Craghorn judged his head was far too hazy to fire Daisy safely past a sobbing Klangor, and instead stumbled as quickly as he could toward the cephalyx. Behind Klangor howled once more as the slaver resumed its assault, and Claghorn was forced to grit his teeth as psychic feedback lashed his own mind and had him seeing stars. For a moment he staggered, but then reached inwards upon his arcane reserves to shake off the effects.
Occupied in dominating Klangor, the cephalyx realized its predicament all too late. Swung with all of Craghorn’s remaining strength, Vulcan struck the creature in the flank. The slaver’s slender body offered very little resistance as the creature crumpled and collapsed to the ground in an awkward angle. Craghorn took no chances, and stamped his boot into its oversized skull. He knew others might have considered that excessive, but he had dealt with the mind slavers before, and knew they deserved little short of the same vicious treatment they inflicted upon others.

name: Name
body:
The exchange had taken less than a minute, and been entirely bloodless for the trollkin. Nonetheless, they all looked at each other warily in the aftermath, as their senses returned to some semblance of normality.
They had now unequivocally crossed into enemy territory. The logical action was to retreat back the way they’d come, and report their discovery. Yet, Craghorn was sure that there was something else, that had gone unseen. Cryxians didn’t normally launch covert raids, and they’d yet to see traces of a single rotter, beyond ambiguous tracks in the mud.
Looking at each of his soldiers, Craghorn knew they were thinking the same. None of them wanted to give up the chase yet. "Right then. Move out."
***
Leaving the cephalyx corpses where they had fallen, the trollkin resumed their march through the tunnels. Unlike the caution from before, however, now they beat a hasty passage. Even without Dutch’s use of explosives, the sound of the fighting had been loud enough to alert anything nearby. They needed to get as deep into the warren as possible before any other patrols came upon them.

name: Name
body:
After another hour or so, the tunnel opened into a wide cavern, that was faintly lit by a slither of daylight eking its way through a crack in the rock above. The ground became a carpet of sand, dim gold in the daylight and softening the sound of their footsteps. Patches of green vegetation spotted the surface, a welcome change after so much time amidst bare and hard rock. The air was warmer here, and only now did Craghorn realise how cold he’d felt while traversing the more claustrophobic passages.
The change in their environment came with a sense of relief. As Dutch’s rash actions had demonstrated, their weapons were unsuited to tunnel warfare, and with each step they’d wrestled with the worry they’d eventually find a place where Klangor couldn’t progress and be forced to turn back. The only exceptions to this were Rattles, who looked sadly at his candle, and muttered to himself as he carefully extinguished its flame; and Dutch, who hadn’t been able to meet Craghorn’s gaze since the encounter with the mind slaver.

name: Name
body:
Craghorn kept them moving. There were a multitude of tracks here, and several alcoves that might have been tunnels along the walls. His intuition told him the area felt like a nexus more than a crossroads, and whatever it was they were looking for, it wouldn’t be far now.
His mind returned unbidden to Felleye’s words, from the previous evening.
The trollkin have always fought. As Molgur, then kriels, against the reds and the swans. So much of our past is defined by struggle. We came here to find peace. But what if peace has made us weak? We’re children of the Wurm, as well as the Great Mother.
Now they were approaching battle. Not a small skirmish, not a border conflict. Real battle. War on a scale which the Kithguard had never before experienced, which no one in Western Immoren had seen from the trollkin since the days of the ancient Molgur tribes, when armies of trollkin, ogrun, and barbarians tens of thousands strong had crashed against the walls of the first cities.
Craghorn’s history was one filled with regrets. He was by nature, restless, moody, and prone to bouts of anger or melancholy. The only place he’d ever felt at home was in the trenches. Between battles, his own demons gnawed at him too vigorously for him to relax. In such moments he felt spiky and his skin crawled, like an addict in search of his next fix. His only saving grace was that he knew himself well enough to know his own weaknesses, and to mitigate them until the time for fighting came once more. This was how he had remained a soldier, and not a burned out wreck, drunk and dying in a back alley somewhere.

name: Name
body:
It was also why he would probably never rise above the rank of sergeant, and never wanted to in any case. If it weren’t for his natural talents as a warlock, he probably wouldn’t lead at all. For the rest of his days, he would be happy just fighting, side by side with the men and women under his command. That was all he really wanted. It was only in war that he was truly at peace.
The dark truth that Craghorn never dared speak aloud was that for him, the return of the Cryx was a blessing of sorts. Upon their arrival, things had changed in the Southern Kriels. An existential threat now existed. It was terrible and gnawed at the pit of his stomach. But it also made him feel alive.
That was the answer to Rudd Felleye’s question. But Craghorn doubted that the sniper would welcome it.
Ahead, Rattles stopped marching and held still, his head cocked as though he was listening for something. "Somefin’s off wit’ the dirt." He dropped to one knee, palm pressed to the ground. "It’s shakin’. Not like wen boots march. Like… water. Tides." The pyg shuddered. Clearly the sea held some sort of fear for him.

name: Name
body:
Dyhllan appeared before Craghorn could press Rattles any further. "Sarge, you’d better take a look at this. Felleye’s found something." The Scrapper wore a concerned expression. "Something weird."
The team convened on Felleye, who had taken point and ranged deeper into the cavern. He’d found a tall arch with a circular opening, cleft from grey stone. Strange symbols had been chiseled into the surface, although their origins were entirely alien to anything that Craghorn or any of the rest of his unit had seen before. They almost looked like they’d flowed into the stone, rather than been carved, so elegant was the curvature of the glyphs. A strange pressure began to build behind the eyes if you stared at them for too long, forcing the observer to cast their gaze elsewhere in submission.
A humanoid face had been sculpted at the highest point of the arch, the expression etched in a pained scream. The eyes were rough voids, as though they had been carefully fashioned and then torn out.
Rattles crossed his arms and defiantly spat at the structure. "Bloody thing. This is what’s causin’ the dirt to shake."

name: Name
body:
The pyg’s saliva hit the surface, but instead of dripping downwards, began to slide inwards, the phlegm scraping across the stone towards the central opening. A faint rushing sound whistled through Craghorn’s ears, as the surrounding air followed suit, soon joined by trails of sand along the ground.
"What is this thing?" Dutch shouted over the din, as the sharp whistle grew to a powerful rush of wind, tearing at their uniforms and dragging them closer.
Great trails of sand and chunks of stone buffeted the trollkin from behind, unbalancing them as they unsuccessfully tried to move away. Rattles was dangerously close to the arch, his knuckles pale blue as he scrabbled at the stone. Craghorn leapt forward to grab the diminutive pyg,  but in doing so was swept in himself. He heard Klangor roar, the sound coming from far, far away, and felt a stab of tremendous rage echo through his mind.
Then…

name: Name
body: Then nothing. The total absence of all existence. The being was alone. Its senses ceased to be, consciousness untethered from the leaden lump that had been its flesh. Through its thoughts it tried to look at itself, and inferred a mental image of a pitted slab of stone, chipped and cracked at the edges to reveal sedimentary layers beneath. It might have understood fear then, if fear existed in this place. The question felt abstract. Answers were irrelevant, a memory of a prior existence. The being— Craghorn crashed face first into the dirt. His entire body ached, like every muscle had been stretched on a rack for hours. His neck felt sticky and wet around the ears, and after dabbing at it, his fingertips came back bloody. His lungs burned, as though they had been deprived of air. After long moments taking deep breaths and gathering his strength, Craghorn slowly pushed himself to a sitting position. Through swimming vision, he saw familiar shapes, all hues of blue and green. Blinking the fog away, the faces of Dutch, Felleye, and Annar swam into view, Rattles sitting between them. The shirts of all three were stained red where their ears had bled, he noticed. When he felt able, Craghorn crawled to their position, and limbs still numb, sat dumbly alongside, willing his mind to slowly reconnect with the world.

name: Name
body:
Dyhllan and Klangor arrived after a time, materializing out of thin air and landing in a confused heap. The latter’s maw was set in a goofy smile, its mind become an impossible jumble of emotions and sensations that would have confused the most experienced of shamans.
Eventually, Craghorn felt composed enough to speak. "Sound—sound off." His voice lacked its normal depth, he noticed. The others replied, in stilted voices and varied tones that told him they too were experiencing the same after effects of travelling through the gate as he was.
Looking around, Craghorn realized for the first time that they were no longer underground. Above, the sky stretched for miles. Surrounding him in all directions was bleak brown rock, without a trace of jungle foliage. In the distance, he could see a row of mountains, colored the same earthy tones as the stone. In stark contrast to the jungle, where every surface was teeming with life, there didn’t seem to be a hint of anything even close to that as far as the eye could see.

name: Name
body:
Without any concept of where they were, Craghorn needed to get his bearings. Moving slowly on complaining limbs, he managed to find his feet. From a standing position, he realized they were atop the rim of a vast crater, the ground a few feet away dipping first into a slight depression, before then plummeting downwards in a sheer slope.
The sound of industry came from within the void below, rising upwards through the air. Wary of being detected, Craghorn crawled on his belly towards the edge, a sense of apprehension dawning upon him. It was justified, he realized, when he reached the edge and could look over. What he saw was sufficient to turn his blood cold.
Dark shapes writhed within the pit below, as rotters crawled around the depression like ants around a nest. Most were engaged in dragging steel sheets, heavy brick, or strange blackened machinery. Others either excavated the earth, kicking up great mounds of dirt and dusty air, or welded pieces of metal together, showing their bodies in sparks. Surrounding them was a den of trenches of varying depths, forming what seemed to be the foundations of some immense edifice in the making. A row of drums sat on the opposite side, a series of pipes running from them and into various ditches. The stench of death was ripe in the air, from the necrotite and so many corpses all in the same space.

name: Name
body:
"Trouble?" Felleye joined Craghorn, hunkering down by his side. Craghorn nodded, as Felleye took in the construction site below, shaking his head in disbelief. "It’s like they’re building a city," the sniper mumbled to himself.
"Not a city. I’ve seen the likes of this before, in the Thornwood." Craghorn corrected him. "It’s a necropolis. That’s what they’re building. And if we can’t stop them, then Dhunia save us all."
